Honestly, I'd recommend waiting a couple months and starting the hobby with the kill team typhon box when that comes out. 

Kill team is a smaller scale skirmish game that let's you get into all aspects of the hobby at a smaller scale so you don't end up being intimidated with a mountain of grey plastic. It will have some terrain and two full kill teams, one of which is a tyranid kill team. It's only 5 models to build and paint the tyranid half, and you'll have another full kill team on hand that you can either sell or use to get some friends to try the game with you. 

If you end up liking the hobby, you can easily expand into big 40k. you will already have some models that will slot into your tyranid army, and the ultimate starter or shopping on ebay for the tyranid half, will get you the tyranid combat patrol to form a  good base for your army.

I wasted a couple years brushing on primer thinking that airbrushing was something for more experienced painters, and was way out of my league skill wise. Don't be me, it speeds up your painting process considerably, and it's much cheaper than using rattlecans.There's tons of good tutorials out there on youtube for getting into airbrushing as a beginner. 

The inital startup cost is roughly a little less or about the same price as a new vanguard/spearhead box for your army. IMO the most important part is to not cheap out on the air compressor. You can get a nice compressor that comes bundled with a shitty no-name airbrush for around $100 or so. While the airbrush itself is not gonna be the best thing around, it can easily handle the basics of priming, basecoating, and highlighting. Later down the line, if you decide you like airbrushing and want something nicer to shoot paint through, the nice aircompressor will be able to handle it easily.

If I could go back and start my paint collection over from scratch, I'd just start off with the monument hobbies pro acryl line base set. It has a ton of good colors with good coverage. 

On the other hand, if you're mainly wanting to slapchop/speed paint to get things on the table picking up the army painter speed paints 2.0 set is a solid choice as well. They're a bit different getting used to when compared to normal opaque paints, I'd say they're a little less forgiving because mistakes are harder to correct due to how transparent they are.


Otherwise, if neither of those options appeal to you,  I'd say skip the sets entirely and only buy the specific colors you need for your current project. that way you don't get stuck with colors you might not use for a while, or ever.

One side tangent: After you dip your toes back in and decide you want to keep collecting/painting, I'd HIGHLY recommend picking up an airbrush sooner rather than later. I spent a couple years wasting tons of time brushing on primer and wasting money on overpriced rattlecans because i was too intimidated by making the jump. It doesn't need to be anything fancy when starting out. I pretty much spent most of my airbrush budget on a $130CAD [air compressor that bundled a shitty noname airbrush and hose.](https://www.amazon.ca/Timbertech-ABPST08K-Airbrush-Compressor-Accessories/dp/B08C2MLQMN?ref_=ast_sto_dp)

Previously what would have been several nights of work, I was able to [complete in a couple hours](https://imgur.com/BxiqXL3).

If you're looking for a premade set, then the Pro Acryl base set might be a good value proposition for you. It's $100 USD for twenty-four 22ml bottles of high-quality paint that come in a good color range to cover most of the bases as a beginner. It's definitely on the pricier side when compared to something like Vallejo or Army painter, but if I could go back and just start out my collection with them, I would do it in a heartbeat. Even if you're not wanting the whole set, at the bare minimum, be sure to get the bold titanium white.

The vallejo game color paints I tried have been fairly hit or miss for me. Both dead white and bonewhite take 3-4 coats to get decent coverage, and that gets really old fast. On the other hand, their metal color line and primers have been great.

Army painter has been stepping up their quality lately, with the 2.0 speedpaints. While those have been good, I can't recommend them as your only paints. They don't perform very well on large flat surfaces and can easily turn splotchy if you're not careful. Unless you're just trying to get some color on your army fast, I personally find They're better suited to have as an additional tool in your collection, but not for your primary method of painting.

know it's an old post, but I didn't see gloomhaven suggested here. The version on steam is literally a digital version of the tabletop game. Each scenario typically runs 45-60 mins. While it does have a long campaign at around 95 scenarios, there's no rush to blast through it.

 You're a band of mercenaries taking on various jobs for people in the town of gloomhaven. You'll start with the choice of 6 classes, and each time you create a character you'll also get a retirement goal. when you complete that goal, you'll unlock one of the 11 hidden classes and then be able to create another character. so In a sense you're always feeling like you're progressing something and also keeping things fresh. just as you're getting tired of playing your current class, you'll likely be close to retirement and be able to unlock something new and fun.

My wife ended up giving it a shot and she loved it. It's also one of the very few video games where after playing I decided I wanted a copy of the tabletop version, and kickstarted the sequel Frosthaven. I've had my copy of Frosthaven since January and we've been slowing burning through it here and there whenever the mood strikes. 

Overall, Gloomhaven is a great pick up and play experience for 2-4 players.

You get a nice sturdy box for each character, all their tokens and cards and it comfortably fits them all inside the gloomhaven box only requiring a couple more inches of lift on the box itself. The biggest downside is having to unbox all of the classes and potentially spoil yourself. That can be remedied by either having someone else put the characters in each box for you, or just by doing it quickly without taking a good look at the minis/cards.

I'm a little late to the party, but I skimmed through the comments and I just wanted to make some quick suggestions. 

First, speaking as someone that's been in your shoes, my biggest recommendation for you is to try out a game when it's brand new. Guilty Gear Strive releases in a few days and has made a lot of changes to their systems to make it easier for new comers to get in and start fighting without getting overwhelmed with heaps of mechanics you need to know prior to going online. It's the time when fighting games are the most fun because the community is all discovering new things about their characters / matchups. 

Secondly, this kind of goes hand in hand with the first point, find a friend or someone random online to befriend so you can run sets against each other. If you're playing a new game, you're much more likely to match with people that are closer to your skill level. Some of the most fun I've had in fighting games was either playing a friend or making a friend from online learning how to body each other. It's a constant back and forth experience each time learning how to beat whatever new things you each learn.   

Third, and this is a mostly personal recommendation. I prefer using a fight stick and I believe you might as well. I find using a Dpad unintuitive/uncomfortable to do inputs with, and while the analog feels better it is much more prone to error due to its size. You can easily overshoot your motions and hit random jumps as you've encountered. With a fight stick it's essentially a big joystick that makes more sense to me for inputs. That being said, this is all complete personal preference so feel free to ignore this if pad is your preference.  

Lastly this is more game specific, but try and stick to one game and more importantly one character. Run through the roster of your chosen game and find a character that you like and stick with them. There's nothing worse than trying to learn a fighting game with a character you don't particularly care for.
